title: Scikit-Learn (Part 20)
content:
I read Aurélien Géron's *Hands-On Machine Learning* chapter by chapter, ran its notebooks on my Mac, and wrote up what I saw. This is the short version, for anyone who has not read the nineteen posts: what I learned, what I would still use, and what I would skip. It has no notebook of its own. Everything here comes from the posts, which have the numbers.

## The main lessons

- **Judge a model on data it has not seen.** A model can memorise what it learned from and look perfect. A decision tree scored an error of $0 on its own training houses, and $67,153 on new ones ([Part 2](/posts/sklearn2/)).
- **Compare with a simple guess first.** A program that says "not a 5" for every handwritten digit is right 91% of the time, and "the same as last week" was hard to beat when forecasting train boardings ([Part 3](/posts/sklearn3/), [Part 15](/posts/sklearn15/)).
- **Most of machine learning is one idea.** Start with random numbers, work out which way each should move to be less wrong, move it a little, and repeat. The rest of the series is where the direction comes from, and what "wrong" means.
- **Fixes can be small and decisive.** Telling a review model to ignore padding took it from 50.0% to 87.5% ([Part 16](/posts/sklearn16/)).
- **Training is fragile.** A picture-drawing model drew one shirt 32 times, and agents reached the top score and then fell away ([Part 17](/posts/sklearn17/), [Part 18](/posts/sklearn18/)).

## How every model learned

There turned out to be only four ways to find a model's numbers.

| Way of learning | Parts | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Worked out exactly | [1](/posts/sklearn1/), [2](/posts/sklearn2/), [5](/posts/sklearn5/), [8](/posts/sklearn8/) | A formula or a solver gives the answer in one calculation, such as the best straight line through points. |
| Remembered | [1](/posts/sklearn1/) | The model stores its training data, and does its work when it is asked a question. |
| Grown | [6](/posts/sklearn6/), [7](/posts/sklearn7/) | A flowchart of yes-or-no questions is built one question at a time, and groups of them vote. |
| Nudged | [3](/posts/sklearn3/), [4](/posts/sklearn4/), [9](/posts/sklearn9/), [10](/posts/sklearn10/) to [19](/posts/sklearn19/) | Every number is moved a little in the direction that makes the answers less wrong, many times over. |

Nudging first appears in Part 3, and is explained in Part 4. From Part 10 on, almost everything is nudged. For a straight line, the direction comes from a formula. For a network with many layers, it comes from a method called backpropagation. What "wrong" means changes too: for a classifier it compares the answer with a label, for a picture-copying network the picture with itself, for a language model the next letter with the real one, which is what my [MiniGPT](/posts/minigpt-grown/) does, and for reinforcement learning the value of an action with the reward that followed it.

## What I would still use

I wrote "still used?" answers in several parts, and they add up to a picture. This is my reading, from what I ran, and from what I know of the field.

| Still a good first choice | Why |
|---|---|
| The workflow of [Part 2](/posts/sklearn2/) | Setting aside a test set, trying a simple baseline, and scoring on held-back data matter for every model. |
| The scores of [Part 3](/posts/sklearn3/) | Precision and recall show what accuracy alone hides. |
| Nudging and its settings ([Part 4](/posts/sklearn4/)) | Everything after it is built on it. |
| Forests of trees, and boosting ([Parts 6](/posts/sklearn6/) and [7](/posts/sklearn7/)) | For tables of data, they are often the best tool. |
| Squeezing data and finding groups ([Parts 8](/posts/sklearn8/) and [9](/posts/sklearn9/)) | Everyday tools for looking at data and making it smaller. |
| The standard tricks for deep networks ([Part 11](/posts/sklearn11/)) | They are the defaults of modern libraries. |
| Retraining someone else's network ([Parts 11](/posts/sklearn11/) and [14](/posts/sklearn14/)) | It beat training from scratch in my runs. |
| Attention ([Part 16](/posts/sklearn16/)) | The design behind today's language models. |

| Good to understand, less likely to use | Why |
|---|---|
| The widest-street method of [Part 5](/posts/sklearn5/) | Niche now, though the picture is a good one. |
| Several methods for unrolling curved data ([Part 8](/posts/sklearn8/)) | Mostly historical. |
| TensorFlow loops, data pipelines, and serving ([Parts 12](/posts/sklearn12/), [13](/posts/sklearn13/), and [19](/posts/sklearn19/)) | The ideas carry over, but much of the field has moved to PyTorch. |
| Networks that carry a memory along a sequence ([Parts 15](/posts/sklearn15/) and [16](/posts/sklearn16/)) | Attention replaced them for language. |
| Networks that forge pictures against a detective ([Part 17](/posts/sklearn17/)) | Diffusion has largely taken over. |

The book was not padding. It is a survey, and a survey includes what was current when it was written. But I would not spend equal time on every chapter.

## What I would do differently

I would run the long trainings at full length from the start. In [Part 16](/posts/sklearn16/) and [Part 17](/posts/sklearn17/) I first shortened the longest ones to save time, and the results were poor: a picture-drawing model that made one picture, and another that made dark blurs. Rerunning at full length fixed most of that, but it took hours, and I did not rerun the translation models. My Mac has a graphics processor, and I tried it: for these small models, with batches of 32, it was slower than the processor, as [Part 12](/posts/sklearn12/) shows. A bigger machine, or bigger batches, is where a graphics processor would help.

I did write the training loop of Part 12 in PyTorch, as well as in TensorFlow, because the loop that I wrote by hand in MiniGPT is in PyTorch. The two gave the same results.
